new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Lou with an empty rule (catalog-all-2026-09-12) and no existing statements; this thesis supplies a rule (weight-sensitive, heaviest syllable, no tone) and the stress domain for compounds vs serial verbs. It matches the same author's 1992 Organised Phonology Data sheet already held by the project ("Stress is predictable. The heaviest syllable in the word attracts stress.", p. 3), and it adds the explicit weight ranking of syllable types, which the OPD does not give.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No contrastive tone. Primary stress is predictable and falls on the heaviest syllable of the word, with the weight scale (C)V < (C)VV < (C)VC < CVVC (onsets do not count). Because non-final syllables tend to be open and final syllables are frequently closed, the rule puts stress on the final syllable in most polysyllables. The one worked example, ak'mat 'fall and die' (VC + CVC, equal weight, stress on the second syllable), suggests the rightmost of equally heavy syllables wins, though the thesis does not state a tie-break explicitly. The domain is the phonological word: a lexicalised compound verb has one primary stress, whereas each verb in a nuclear-layer serial verb construction keeps its own primary stress (a'pur 'ngan 'cook eat'), and this stress test is the author's criterion for distinguishing compounds from SVCs (pp. 107-108, 144).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Monosyllabic verb roots that compound (ak + mat > ak'mat) lose their individual stress and take a single primary stress; verbs in a series each retain primary stress. Footnote 40 leaves open whether compounds are a different nexus type of nuclear juncture.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Lou of Lou Island, Manus Province, PNG (Oceanic, Admiralties), the same variety as the author's 1992 SIL OPD sheet (Lako village data checked September 1992). No dialect subdivision is discussed in the phonology overview.

readall_conflicts: Within this task's works there is only one source, so no conflict among them. Against material already saved in our check folder from the 2026-09-16 pass: Stutzman's 1992 OPD sheet (p. 3) agrees with the thesis exactly (predictable stress on the heaviest syllable). Blust 1998, A Lou vocabulary (sec. 2.4.3 Stress, printed p. 57) reports instead that "In citation forms primary stress generally was recorded on the final syllable. However, in a number of cases I also recorded penultimate stress", and himself calls the emphatic-vs-context explanation "speculative". Blust's positional description (final, sometimes penult) differs in type from Stutzman's weight rule, but the two are largely reconcilable: Stutzman notes that non-final syllables tend to be open and final syllables are frequently closed, so the heaviest-syllable rule predicts final stress in most words, and Blust's penultimate cases could be words whose final syllable is light; neither source discusses the other's account, and Blust's record is impressionistic rather than an analysis. Stutzman (two works, SIL fieldworker with checked data) is the better-supported reading.

sources.quote: 'In citation forms primary stress generally was recorded on the final syllable peak. However, in a number of cases I also recorded penultimate stress. It is possible that the former is an emphatic pattern, characteristic of forms offered in isolation, while the latter is more typical of forms in sentence context, but this remains speculative.' Also notes short sentences merging into one phonological word with penultimate stress ([ŋapaŋkalamimiʔ], stress on penult of /mimi/).
